Book 2 has no distinctions in this EDF (it is a flat list of questions), so no Book 2 Distinctio 44 exists; other divs have no interpreted children and are omitted.

wo8uy7-d1e64.summary: The Prologue to Book I is Ockham's theory of theological knowledge, set out in twelve questions: four principal questions, each followed by annexed questions. (1) Can the wayfarer have evident knowledge of theological truths? (q1) Here Ockham lays the epistemological foundation of the whole work. He distinguishes apprehension from judgment and intuitive from abstractive cognition, the latter two being specifically distinct cognitions of the same object, differing intrinsically. Intuition is the cognition by which one can evidently know whether a thing exists. It extends to sensible singulars and to one's own mental acts, and by divine power even to non-existents. He concludes that God could give a wayfarer distinct abstractive knowledge of deity and so evident knowledge of some necessary theological truths, but not of contingent ones such as the Incarnation. (2) Is such evident knowledge strict science? (q2) He defines the strictly knowable as necessary, doubtable and syllogistically evidenced, explains how experience and a uniformity principle yield universal principles, and against Scotus argues that nothing intrinsic to God is demonstrable of the divine essence known in itself. Only common connotative or negative concepts can be demonstrated of God, through common middles. The annexed questions refine his theory of demonstration. Properties as second-mode predicates are concepts that connote something really distinct; connotative abstracts have only a nominal definition (q3). Absolute inherent properties are known of their first subject only by experience (q4). The middle of demonstration is sometimes, not always, the subject's definition, with an account of real and nominal definitions (q5). Every simply necessary proposition is per se in the first or second mode, and first-mode propositions can be known by science in a broad sense (q6). (3) Is theology as we have it under the common law strict science? (q7) No. Articles of faith are not self-evident, derivable or known by experience. Conclusions cannot be known from merely believed principles, against Aquinas's subalternation model. Apart from faith, a believing theologian has no habit an unbeliever could not have. The annexed questions argue that theology is not one habit but an ordered aggregate of really distinct habits proportioned to acts (q8). God under the ratio of deity is not the subject of our theology; its suppositing subject is a proper composite concept of God, and different parts have God, the persons or creatures as subjects. This rests on a deflationary account of a science's subject as simply the subject of its conclusions, against Scotus's 'virtual containment' (q9). (4) Is theology practical or speculative? (q12) After preliminary questions on praxis (q10) and on what distinguishes practical from speculative knowledge (q11), he answers that theology contains distinct cognitions, some speculative (God is triune) and some practical (God is to be loved). Knowledge is practical when praxis or its product is a total or partial object. Praxis is primarily the will's free act and can include chosen speculation; sciences are distinguished by their known conclusions rather than their subjects or ends. Throughout, Ockham opposes Scotus and Aquinas, argues for parsimony, intuitive cognition, connotation and real distinction among habits, and limits what the wayfarer can know of God to what is reached through common and composite concepts.
claims: The wayfarer can, by divine power, have evident knowledge of some necessary theological truths, but not of contingent ones like the Incarnation.
Intuitive and abstractive cognition are specifically distinct cognitions of the same object; intuition grounds evident knowledge of contingent existence, including of one's own mental acts.
Strict science is evident knowledge of a necessary, doubtable truth caused by syllogistic discourse, so God lacks it in that sense.
Theology as we have it under the common law is not strict science of the articles of faith.
Theology is an aggregate of distinct habits, not one science, and has no single subject; our concepts of God are composite and connotative.
Theology is partly speculative and partly practical, depending on whether its propositions have praxis as an object.

wo8uy7-d1e1658.summary: Distinction 37 of Book I has a single question: whether being everywhere and in all things by essence, presence and power belongs properly to God alone. Ockham accepts the theological conclusion but rejects grounding God's essential presence in his immediate causality. An argument about sunlight on a shaded body shows that agents can act immediately at a distance, so causing something does not entail being in it. He analyzes the modes of presence: by power, by cognitive or spatial presence, and by essence (non-distance, as form is in matter), along with God's special presence by grace and by union. He argues that God is in all things by each mode. What is uniquely divine is not de facto ubiquity, which God could grant a creature, but that the existence of any thing entails God's presence in it. The replies add distinctions of 'per essentiam' and a supposition-based denial that universals are everywhere.
claims: Action at a distance is possible, so causality does not entail presence.
God is in all things by power, presence and essence.
What is proper to God alone is that the existence of anything entails God's presence in it.
By divine power a creature could in fact be present in all other creatures.

wo8uy7-d1e59.summary: Partial summary: of the 49 direct divisions of Book I in the EDF, this rests only on the Prologue and Distinction 37, not on Distinctions 1–36 or 38–48. So far as these show, Book I opens with Ockham's epistemology of theology. The Prologue covers intuitive and abstractive cognition, evident knowledge, the conditions of strict science and demonstration, whether theology is a science (it is not, under the common law), its lack of unity and of a single subject, and its mixed practical and speculative character. Distinction 37 applies his conceptual tools to divine omnipresence: action at a distance, analysis of the modes of presence, and what is uniquely proper to God. Common to both are his rejection of standard Scotist and Thomist positions, his reliance on divine absolute power as a test of real distinction and separability, and his semantic analysis of terms such as 'per essentiam', connotative names and concepts of God. Nothing here should be taken as a summary of Book I's treatment of the Trinity, divine attributes, knowledge, will or predestination in the uncovered distinctions.
claims: Book I opens with an epistemology of theological knowledge (Prologue).
In the covered parts Ockham consistently uses divine omnipotence, intuitive cognition and semantic analysis against Scotist and Thomist positions.

wo8uy7.summary: Partial summary: this rests only on Book I, itself covered only through its Prologue and Distinction 37; Books II, III and IV are not covered. On that narrow basis, the Scriptum in libros sententiarum (Ockham's Ordinatio) begins by settling what kind of knowledge theology can be. Ockham argues that the wayfarer reaches God only through composite and connotative concepts, that theology is not strict science of the articles of faith but an aggregate of habits including faith, and that it is partly practical and partly speculative. This rests on a theory of intuitive and abstractive cognition. In the one distinction covered beyond the Prologue, the same analytic methods are used on divine omnipresence. No claims are made here about the content of the uncovered books or distinctions.
claims: The work opens by defining theology's epistemic status: not strict science, but an aggregate of habits including faith.
Its method, in the covered portions, combines a theory of cognition, semantic analysis and appeal to divine absolute power.
